title: Getting up after failure
tomorrow: Gurpreet uncle's warehouse just closed. what does the sangat do?

cards: The grade portal refreshes, and there it is: a 54 on the chemistry test. Simran stares at it in the school hallway while people push past.
By lunch she has a plan, and the plan is to drop chemistry, drop the summer program, maybe drop engineering altogether.
Maya reads the plan, then sends a photo of a magnet on her grandma's fridge, a Bible verse in old-fashioned letters. Simran texts back: ok but what does Sikhi say about bombing a test?

teach.b: Guru Nanak answers on Ang 61, in paraphrase: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never err. That's the starting line.
Falling short isn't a surprise to be ashamed of; it's the human condition, written into the Guru Granth Sahib. Nobody on the path is the exception. So the question isn't whether you fall.
It's where you turn when you do: back toward the Guru, and back to the work. Now the fridge magnet.
It's from Proverbs, chapter twenty-four, in the King James words: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again."
That's the shared thing, and it's a real one: two traditions that expect people to fall, and point to rising, not to never falling.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: a verse on a Christian fridge and a line from Guru Nanak both start by assuming you'll fall. And the honest difference.
Proverbs sets the rising man beside the wicked who stumble into trouble, and makes getting up a mark of the just.
Guru Nanak puts every human on the same side, all erring, and the only one who doesn't err is the Guru. Simran doesn't drop chemistry. She emails her teacher about office hours, and goes on Tuesday.

how: Sikhs who fall short bring it to Ardas and begin again; a Sikh who breaks the code of conduct can go before the Panj Pyare, accept a tankhah (a penance) and start fresh.

games.q: what does “getting up after failure” mean?
o: turning back to the Guru and the work after you fall
quitting the thing that went wrong to stay safe
proving you never really failed in the first place

games.q: a bad grade and a fridge magnet — tap the pairs.
p: falleth seven times, riseth up again

s: Sikhi expects a devoted Sikh never to fail
Ang 61: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never err.
both the Proverbs verse and Guru Nanak's line assume people will fall
the shared hope is in rising, not in never falling.

games.q: a friend from a church family says, 'our Bible says the just man falls seven times and rises. so your Gurus say the same, right?' what's the fairest reply?
o: we share the getting up; Guru Nanak says all err but the Guru.
exactly the same; every religion just says try again.
not really; ours is the deeper teaching about failure.
games.why: name the real shared hope and the honest difference: Proverbs pairs rising with the just, Guru Nanak starts from everyone erring. rank neither.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write by hand one thing you fell short on lately, and under it, one small next step, like an email or a retry. Hold the paper for the sit, and let the second line be the one you read last.

wordCard.voice: Getting up after failure. Everyone errs, Guru Nanak says; the turn is back toward the Guru and back to the work.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: abhul, one who never errs; on Ang 61, only the Guru and the Creator.

carryVoice: For the road: get up, because everyone falls and only the Guru never errs. Day 1721, standing.
